summary: Customer reported a 3-hour cascading delay on inference pipelines during a peak batch window leading to 25% failed requests and increased tail latency. Redwood and NovaRetail did a joint RCA focusing on KV-cache warmup, autoscaling thresholds, and a problematic scheduled job that amplified cold starts. Agreed short-term mitigations (increase min-replicas, adjust prefix cache retention) and longer-term items (caching instrumentation, staged canary config, runbooks).
topics: Follow-up cadence and postmortem doc ownership
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Okay, thanks everyone for joining. We wanted to get through the timeline and propose mitigations. Marta, do you want to start with a quick impact summary?
[00:12] Marta Gonzalez: Sure. On Tuesday at 09:12 local we saw a spike in queued inference requests, the consumer batch hit our peak of about 9k concurrent requests and latency started to climb, eventually a lot of requests timed out, so roughly three hours of degraded throughput. About 25 percent of user calls failed or fell back.
[00:30] Samir Das: To add, we also had a data-sync cron that was kicking off full table snapshot to staging, that increased I/O and caused our staging cluster to hit higher memory, which then seemed to trigger a scale-down upstream.
[00:45] Priya Patel: Right, the interesting piece we saw on the Redwood side is the KV cache had a low hit rate during the window. The prefix cache warmup didn't populate as fast as expected after the autoscaler oscillated.
[01:02] Liam O'Neal: Is that the K V cache you mean? I ask because our internal logs show cache misses spiking in tandem with pod restarts.
[01:12] Ethan Wu: Yeah; sometimes the recorder shows "K-V cash" in the metric names, we've seen transcription typos in other runs, but the actual metric is kv_cache_hit_ratio. The sequence we observed: scale-to-zero, then burst traffic, then multiple replicas booting and missing the hot prefixes, so each new replica had to rebuild large KV state.
[01:35] Rachel Chen: From compliance I've got a quick question — did any of the failed requests involve PII scanning or redaction? We need to know if anything escaped logging retention.
[01:45] Marta Gonzalez: We did a sample — no PII was returned. Requests were failing at network timeout layer. But logs were partial, some entries missing due to log-rate throttling.
[01:58] Alex Morgan: Let's walk timeline: 09:12 first latency climb, 09:20 autoscaler started to remove replicas because CPU trending below threshold on older pods, then 09:25 a scheduled job increased IO, 09:28 burst arrived, by 09:30 new pods started with cold kv loads. Between 09:30 and 11:45 we saw progressive tail latency increases.
[02:20] Priya Patel: We captured staged traces, see file link in chat: https://redwood.example/trace/ntv-20260805 (note: placeholder link). The traces show repeated large KV fetches that were blocking token generation threads. The kernel-level scheduling is fine, but the runtime hit an unexpected hot-set rehydration.
[02:45] Samir Das: On our side we have autoscaler tuned to target CPU 60 percent and min-replicas=1 to save cost. That left the cluster vulnerable to scale-down on non-peak micro-bursts.
[03:00] Liam O'Neal: Correct, you'd need a buffer. We thought the min idle per zone would handle it but apparently not.
[03:08] Ethan Wu: Two immediate mitigations we recommend: bump min-replicas to 3 during business hours and enable prefix-cache persistent snapshot restore so new pods can rehydrate quickly. Also temporarily increase request timeout from 60s to 90s to avoid user-visible failures.
[03:28] Marta Gonzalez: That makes sense. What's the risk of increased cost if we raise min-replicas?
[03:33] Priya Patel: We estimate roughly 18-22 percent increase in infra spend during business hours. But it avoids customer-facing failures; cost vs availability tradeoff.
[03:44] Rachel Chen: For our security posture, we need the snapshot restore to be encrypted and KMS-backed. Is that supported?
[03:51] Ethan Wu: Yes, Redwood supports KMS integration and encrypted snapshots; we'll include the SOC2 addendum and key management flow in the packet.
[04:02] Alex Morgan: (to-do) I'll send the compliance packet after this call.
[04:06] Samir Das: Another question — that scheduled data-sync, can we throttle it or shift it out of business hours?
[04:12] Marta Gonzalez: We can move it but it's part of nightly reconciliation. We actually found it was mis-scheduled for a one-off run during the business window. That was human error on our change calendar.
[04:23] Priya Patel: Good catch. So we have three contributors: scheduler misfire, low min-replicas, and lack of persistent prefix snapshots.
[04:34] Liam O'Neal: Also the autoscaler threshold is CPU-based; because inference is often memory/IO-bound, CPU didn't reflect actual load. We should consider a custom metric (e.g., kv_cache_miss_rate or queue_length).
[04:48] Ethan Wu: Agreed. We can help set up HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) on the queue depth metric or use Redwood's request queue metric for scaling.
[05:00] Marta Gonzalez: For the short-term rollouts, we want a clear rollback plan. If we bump min-replicas and that causes cost spikes or other issues, how do we revert quickly?
[05:10] Priya Patel: Revert is straightforward: change min-replicas back and clear the snapshot restore flag. But the tricky bit is if the system has already warmed the cache, when we scale down we'll lose benefits. So we plan: 1) enable persistent restore, 2) scale to min=3, 3) monitor for 2 hours, then evaluate.
[05:30] Alex Morgan: We'll create a canary procedure — Ethan, can you draft the playbook?
[05:35] Ethan Wu: Yep, I'll include steps: pre-checks, validate snapshot integrity, run small ramp-up, watch kv_hit_ratio, and abort criteria. I'll also include rollback commands and required RBAC.
[05:50] Samir Das: About the KV snapshot size — how long does restore take? On our staging it looked like 90 seconds for medium prefix sets, but in prod the state is bigger.
[06:02] Priya Patel: Restore time varies; we saw between 80-240s depending on network and object size. We're working on incremental restore so hot prefixes fetch first. That's part of Redwood Optimize roadmap but not GA yet.
[06:18] Rachel Chen: We need an audit trail for any snapshot access. Can Redwood provide an access log for snapshot reads?
[06:25] Ethan Wu: Yes, snapshots are logged; we'll include the S3 access logs and KMS decrypt events as part of the packet.
[06:33] Alex Morgan: Quick note — competitors were brought up in earlier threads. Marta, did you mention VendorX had an on-demand warm pool?
[06:40] Marta Gonzalez: Yeah, we looked at VendorX and CloudAI-Endpoints; VendorX maintains spare warm instances which reduces cold-start impact but at higher cost. We want a middle ground.
[06:51] Liam O'Neal: Could also use predictive pre-warming based on traffic patterns. We have some weekly traffic predictability which can be leveraged.
[07:00] Priya Patel: For medium-term engineering work: instrument cache warmup with finer-grain metrics, expose kv_cache_prefetch latency, add HPA on queue_depth, and build an automated snapshot rotate/restore test. We'll estimate effort: 2 sprint tasks + 1 spike.
[07:17] Samir Das: On ownership: NovaRetail will handle rescheduling the data-sync and giving sandbox logs. Redwood to provide snapshot commands and canary playbook.
[07:30] Alex Morgan: Great. Let's recap next steps. Priya, you're taking cache snapshot and traces. Ethan will prepare the canary runbook. Samir will share staging IAM. Alex sends SOC2 addendum. Marta reviews runbook and signs off for canary.
[07:47] Marta Gonzalez: One more item — can we have a weekly 30-minute check-in during the mitigation window to catch regressions?
[07:54] Alex Morgan: Yep, let's book a recurring slot for next two weeks.
[08:00] Rachel Chen: Also, I'd like a short note in the postmortem about lessons learned for change calendar controls. That was the primary human trigger.
[08:10] Alex Morgan: Absolutely. We'll include a retro section and action owners.
[08:15] [crosstalk and brief background noise]
[08:25] Ethan Wu: I'll run the canary in eu-west-1 first because the incident was in that region; using smaller traffic sample. Expected duration ~1 hour.
[08:35] Priya Patel: We'll also patch the autoscaler to consider queue length; that requires a metric server update but should be quick.
[08:44] Samir Das: I'll provision a role for read-only staging logs and send details to Alex.
[08:50] Alex Morgan: Perfect. Anything else before we wrap?
[08:54] Marta Gonzalez: No, thanks everyone, this was productive.
[08:58] Alex Morgan: Thanks all — we will send notes and own the postmortem doc. Meeting adjourned.
